fetched_contents.text: Effectiveness of an intervention for reducing sitting time and improving health in office workers: three arm cluster randomised controlled trial Abstract Objectives To evaluate the effectiveness of an intervention, with and without a height adjustable desk, on daily sitting time, and to investigate the relative effectiveness of the two interventions, and the effectiveness of both interventions on physical behaviours and physical, biochemical, psychological, and work related health and performance outcomes. Design Cluster three arm randomised controlled trial with follow-up at three and 12 months. Setting Local government councils in Leicester, Liverpool, and Greater Manchester, UK. Participants 78 clusters including 756 desk based employees in defined offices, departments, or teams from two councils in Leicester, three in Greater Manchester, and one in Liverpool. Interventions Clusters were randomised to one of three conditions: the SMART Work and Life (SWAL) intervention, the SWAL intervention with a height adjustable desk (SWAL plus desk), or control (usual practice). Main outcomes measures The primary outcome measure was daily sitting time, assessed by accelerometry, at 12 month follow-up. Secondary outcomes were accelerometer assessed sitting, prolonged sitting, standing and stepping time, and physical activity calculated over any valid day, work hours, workdays, and non-workdays, self-reported lifestyle behaviours, musculoskeletal problems, cardiometabolic health markers, work related health and performance, fatigue, and psychological measures. Results Mean age of participants was 44.7 years, 72.4% (n=547) were women, and 74.9% (n=566) were white. Daily sitting time at 12 months was significantly lower in the intervention groups (SWAL −22.2 min/day, 95% confidence interval −38.8 to −5.7 min/day, P=0.003; SWAL plus desk −63.7 min/day, −80.1 to −47.4 min/day, P<0.001) compared with the control group. The SWAL plus desk intervention was found to be more effective than SWAL at changing sitting time (−41.7 min/day, −56.3 to −27.0 min/day, P<0.001). Favourable differences in sitting and prolonged sitting time at three and 12 month follow-ups for both intervention groups and for standing time for the SWAL plus desk group were observed during work hours and on workdays. Both intervention groups were associated with small improvements in stress, wellbeing, and vigour, and the SWAL plus desk group was associated with improvements in pain in the lower extremity, social norms for sitting and standing at work, and support. Conclusions Both SWAL and SWAL plus desk were associated with a reduction in sitting time, although the addition of a height adjustable desk was found to be threefold more effective. Two recent large randomised controlled trials evaluated multicomponent interventions to reduce sedentary behaviour involving a height adjustable desk and observed differences of 45 minutes per eight hour workday in sitting time in favour of the intervention compared with control at 12 month follow-up26 27; however, both of these randomised controlled trials focused primarily on reducing sitting time at work and showed no impact on behaviour outside of work. Evidence suggests that office workers also tend to be highly sedentary outside of work,28 and therefore by extending workplace interventions to deal with sedentary behaviour both during work and at other times might potentially achieve greater impacts on health. This is important knowledge for organisations that invest in workplace wellbeing programmes for employees, as the provision of height adjustable desks involves cost. fetched_contents.text: Workplace interventions for reducing sitting at work Abstract Background A large number of people are employed in sedentary occupations. Physical inactivity and excessive sitting at workplaces have been linked to increased risk of cardiovascular disease, obesity, and all‐cause mortality. Objectives To evaluate the effectiveness of workplace interventions to reduce sitting at work compared to no intervention or alternative interventions. Search methods We searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, OSH UPDATE, PsycINFO, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) search portal up to 9 August 2017. We also screened reference lists of articles and contacted authors to find more studies. Selection criteria We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs), cross‐over RCTs, cluster‐randomised controlled trials (cluster‐RCTs), and quasi‐RCTs of interventions to reduce sitting at work. For changes of workplace arrangements, we also included controlled before‐and‐after studies. The primary outcome was time spent sitting at work per day, either self‐reported or measured using devices such as an accelerometer‐inclinometer and duration and number of sitting bouts lasting 30 minutes or more. We considered energy expenditure, total time spent sitting (including sitting at and outside work), time spent standing at work, work productivity and adverse events as secondary outcomes. Data collection and analysis Two review authors independently screened titles, abstracts and full‐text articles for study eligibility. Two review authors independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias. We contacted authors for additional data where required. Main results We found 34 studies — including two cross‐over RCTs, 17 RCTs, seven cluster‐RCTs, and eight controlled before‐and‐after studies — with a total of 3,397 participants, all from high‐income countries. The studies evaluated physical workplace changes (16 studies), workplace policy changes (four studies), information and counselling (11 studies), and multi‐component interventions (four studies). One study included both physical workplace changes and information and counselling components. We did not find any studies that specifically investigated the effects of standing meetings or walking meetings on sitting time. Physical workplace changes Interventions using sit‐stand desks, either alone or in combination with information and counselling, reduced sitting time at work on average by 100 minutes per workday at short‐term follow‐up (up to three months) compared to sit‐desks (95% confidence interval (CI) −116 to −84, 10 studies, low‐quality evidence). The pooled effect of two studies showed sit‐stand desks reduced sitting time at medium‐term follow‐up (3 to 12 months) by an average of 57 minutes per day (95% CI −99 to −15) compared to sit‐desks. Total sitting time (including sitting at and outside work) also decreased with sit‐stand desks compared to sit‐desks (mean difference (MD) −82 minutes/day, 95% CI −124 to −39, two studies) as did the duration of sitting bouts lasting 30 minutes or more (MD −53 minutes/day, 95% CI −79 to −26, two studies, very low‐quality evidence). We found no significant difference between the effects of standing desks and sit‐stand desks on reducing sitting at work. Active workstations, such as treadmill desks or cycling desks, had unclear or inconsistent effects on sitting time. Workplace policy changes We found no significant effects for implementing walking strategies on workplace sitting time at short‐term (MD −15 minutes per day, 95% CI −50 to 19, low‐quality evidence, one study) and medium‐term (MD −17 minutes/day, 95% CI −61 to 28, one study) follow‐up. Short breaks (one to two minutes every half hour) reduced time spent sitting at work on average by 40 minutes per day (95% CI −66 to −15, one study, low‐quality evidence) compared to long breaks (two 15‐minute breaks per workday) at short‐term follow‐up. Information and counselling Providing information, feedback, counselling, or all of these resulted in no significant change in time spent sitting at work at short‐term follow‐up (MD −19 minutes per day, 95% CI −57 to 19, two studies, low‐quality evidence). However, the reduction was significant at medium‐term follow‐up (MD −28 minutes per day, 95% CI −51 to −5, two studies, low‐quality evidence). Computer prompts combined with information resulted in no significant change in sitting time at work at short‐term follow‐up (MD −14 minutes per day, 95% CI −39 to 10, three studies, low‐quality evidence), but at medium‐term follow‐up they produced a significant reduction (MD −55 minutes per day, 95% CI −96 to −14, one study). Furthermore, computer prompting resulted in a significant decrease in the average number (MD −1.1, 95% CI −1.9 to −0.3, one study) and duration (MD ‐74 minutes per day, 95% CI −124 to −24, one study) of sitting bouts lasting 30 minutes or more. Computer prompts with instruction to stand reduced sitting at work on average by 14 minutes per day (95% CI 10 to 19, one study) more than computer prompts with instruction to walk at least 100 steps at short‐term follow‐up. We found no significant reduction in workplace sitting time at medium‐term follow‐up following mindfulness training (MD −23 minutes per day, 95% CI −63 to 17, one study, low‐quality evidence). Similarly a single study reported no change in sitting time at work following provision of highly personalised or contextualised information and less personalised or contextualised information. fetched_contents.text: Objectively Measured Sedentary Behavior and Physical Fitness in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Abstract Background: Sedentary behavior has been considered an independent risk factor to health. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to examine associations between objectively measured sedentary time and physical fitness components in healthy adults. Methods: Four electronic databases (Web of Science, Scopus, Pubmed and Sport Discus) were searched (up to 20 September 2020) to retrieve studies on healthy adults which used observational, cohort and cross-sectional designs. Studies were included if sedentary time was measured objectively and examined associations with the health- or skill-related attributes of physical fitness (e.g., muscular strength, cardiorespiratory fitness, balance). After applying additional search criteria, 21 papers (11,101 participants) were selected from an initial pool of 5192 identified papers. Results: Significant negative associations were found between total sedentary time with cardiorespiratory fitness (r = −0.164, 95%CI: −0.240, −0.086, p < 0.001), muscular strength (r = −0.147, 95%CI: −0.266, −0.024, p = 0.020) and balance (r = −0.133, 95%CI: −0.255, −0.006, p = 0.040). Conclusions: The evidence found suggests that sedentary time can be associated with poor physical fitness in adults (i.e., muscular strength, cardiorespiratory fitness and balance), so strategies should be created to encourage behavioral changes. Keywords: sedentary time, accelerometry, physical capability, performance, cardiorespiratory fitness, strength, adults, meta-analysis 1. Introduction Physical fitness can be defined as a set of health- or skill-related attributes (e.g., cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), muscular strength, balance, flexibility) that persons possess or achieve in order to carry out daily tasks [1]. Lower levels of physical fitness have been associated with a physical disability and loss of independence [2], increased falling risk and fractures [3] and increased risk of diseases with advancing age [4,5]. Furthermore, evidence shows that CRF and musculoskeletal fitness (mainly grip strength) are predictors of morbidity and all-cause mortality among middle-aged and older adults [6,7,8]. Flexibility, another health-related physical fitness component, is associated with better functional state, better ability to perform daily living activities [9] and better quality of life [10]. However, and unlike muscular strength and CRF, flexibility does not predict all-cause mortality [11]. Balance, as a skill-related component, has also been positively associated with functional capacity and can be predictive of physical independence in daily activities with age [12]. Thus, preservation of physical fitness has become a major public health concern, where the potential role of physical activity (PA) in maintaining functional independence and disease prevention has been recognized by many health organizations [4]. In turn, despite several studies supporting the positive association between PA and several health indicators (e.g., physical fitness), sedentary behavior (SB) is considered a new risk factor to health among adults, even after adjusting for PA levels [13,14,15]. SB, which is distinct from physical inactivity, is defined by any waking behavior characterized by an energy expenditure of ≤1.5 metabolic equivalents (METs), while in a sitting, reclining or lying posture [16]. A recent study revealed that adults (aged between 20 and 75 years) of four different European countries presented an average sedentary time (ST) of 8.83 h per day [17]. Available data suggest that ST is detrimental to cardiometabolic health [18] and is associated with increased risk of all-cause mortality in adults [19,20]. Regarding adults’ physical fitness, evidence shows that larger amounts of ST are associated with lower muscular strength [21,22,23,24], lower CRF [25,26,27,28] and lower balance [21,29]. However, other studies demonstrated that ST was not significantly associated with impaired muscular strength [30,31,32] and CRF [33,34,35] in adults. Even though some studies have focused on this topic, the associations between total ST and physical fitness components are still unclear. Moreover, it should be noted that a lot of studies employ subjective measures of ST, which are known to reduce data accuracy significantly, because of misreporting and recall bias [18,36]. Furthermore, cultural and linguistic issues in the interpretation of questions and/or concepts used could make comparability between countries and cultures difficult [17]. Thus, it is advisable to use objective instruments to assess ST, in order to avoid subjective biases [36]. Regarding physical fitness components, Campbell et al. [37] conducted a recent systematic review and meta-analysis to analyze the associations between ST with body weight and composition in adults and concluded that there were no significant associations between SB and any measure of body weight or obesity, with the exception of waist circumference. Thus, body composition (as a component of physical fitness) was not included in our research strategy. Since adults are typically physically inactive [38] and present high levels of SB (in Europe) [17], it is necessary to have a better understanding of the associations between ST and physical fitness. If such detrimental associations are verified, reducing SB can be important in preventing functional limitations and the loss of independence with age [24,39]. To the best of our knowledge, there is currently no systematic review and meta-analysis available that investigates the evidence regarding the associations between objectively measured ST and physical fitness (e.g., CRF, muscular strength, balance, speed, flexibility) in adults. fetched_contents.text: Workplace Intervention for Reducing Sitting Time in Sedentary Workers: Protocol for a Pilot Study Using the Behavior Change Wheel Abstract The workplace is a major contributor to excessive sitting in office workers. There are a wide array of adverse effects of high volumes of sitting time, including an increased risk of type 2 diabetes and depression. Active workstations can be used in effective interventions to decrease workplace sitting. However, there are a lack of interventions that have been developed using a systematic process that is informed by participant needs and a framework for identifying the most appropriate content for the intervention. Applying these methods could increase adherence and potential effectiveness of the intervention. Therefore, the purpose of this pilot study is to examine the feasibility, acceptability, and efficacy of a tailored workplace intervention to reduce and break up sitting in office workers that has been developed using the Behavior Change Wheel and the APEASE (Acceptability, Practicability, Effectiveness/cost-effectiveness, Affordability, Safety/side-effects, Equity) criteria. This article reports the protocol for this study that is currently ongoing. Participants will be cluster-randomized (by offices) to control and intervention groups. The evaluation of the intervention includes determining feasibility by assessing participant recruitment, retention and data completion rates. Adherence to the intervention will be assessed based on daily sitting and standing time relative to guidelines provided to participants as part of the intervention. Outcome measures also include productivity measured using Ecological Momentary Assessment, absenteeism, presenteeism, cardiometabolic risk markers, and wellbeing. The findings of this study will inform the effective design and implementation of interventions for reducing and breaking up sitting in office workers. Keywords: sedentary behavior, Behavior Change Wheel, intervention, desk-based employees, office workers, pilot study, protocol Introduction Sedentary behavior has been described as any waking behavior in a sitting, reclining or lying posture that has an energy expenditure of ≤ 1.5 metabolic equivalents (METs) (1). In the United Kingdom, high levels of sedentary behavior have been reported with male and female employees sitting more than 11 h/day on average (2). Studies have identified the workplace as a major contributor to excessive sitting (3) with one study reporting that office workers spent 79% of their working day sitting and 42% of their work hours engaging in prolonged sitting (i.e., sitting bouts ≥ 30 min) (4). Individuals who spend prolonged periods being sedentary have an increased risk of adverse health outcomes, including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, some cancers, and mental health problems such as depression and anxiety (5–9). This has led to incorporating a focus on reducing and breaking up sedentary behavior in national and international physical activity guidelines (10, 11). As high amounts of sitting are accumulated in the office workplace, this is a key setting where interventions could be implemented to improve occupational and public health. Indeed, an expert consensus statement recommended that workers who are in predominantly desk-based occupations should start by accumulating 2 h of standing and light activity during working hours each day, and progress to reaching a target of 4 h per day (12). There is a growing body of evidence that suggests height-adjustable workstations (i.e., a workstation that permits the user to interchangeably work in a seated or standing posture) could be effective for decreasing sitting in the workplace (13). When height-adjustable workstations are provided as part of multi-component interventions that also include strategies such as education, manager support, standing meetings, self-monitoring and social support, workplace sitting has been significantly reduced by 45 to 83 min/work shift after 12 months (14, 15). Although these interventions appear promising, management of organizations might be reluctant to implement them if productivity is negatively affected (16). With respect to productivity concerns, a systematic review reported that productivity is likely to be unaffected by using a height-adjustable workstation (17). There are also limited studies that have reported taking employee's perceptions and experiences into account when developing interventions to reduce workplace sitting (18), which may limit intervention adherence and effectiveness. By involving the target audience in the development of interventions, this will help to ensure their needs are met and enhance their adherence and engagement (19). The Behavior Change Wheel (BCW) (20, 21) has been recommended for guiding the systematic process of developing an intervention using a framework that takes into account the needs of the target audience. To the author's knowledge, only one previous office workplace intervention has been developed using the BCW (18); the SMArT Work intervention in National Health Service employees led to significant reductions in sitting at work and improvements in job performance, work engagement, occupational fatigue, sickness presenteeism, anxiety and quality of life over 12 months (15). Further research is required in other occupational groups to strengthen the evidence base for incorporating a focus on reducing and breaking up sitting in workplace policy and practice. Demonstrating the effectiveness of such interventions for improving work-related outcomes, such as worker productivity, will be important for encouraging the adoption of such changes in policy and practice. Publication bias and small-study effects can distort conclusions about sedentary behavior interventions by inflating or deflating apparent treatment effects. The evidence here is mixed: one systematic review and meta-analysis reports **low evidence for publication bias** based on funnel plot inspection, but the same source also says the funnel plot “graphically depicts” bias detection methods and that Egger regression is used for Mendelian randomization bias detection [N4-F3]. Another study explicitly reports that **Egger’s tests showed no significant publication bias** for prevalence of sedentary behavior in individuals with obesity and physical inactivity [N4-R2]. In contrast, a separate search result states that a funnel plot was asymmetric and the publication bias was **high** according to Egger’s test [N4-R5]. These results are not directly comparable because the latter is a different study and topic, so they should be interpreted cautiously.

The direction of distortion depends on the nature of missing studies. If smaller studies are missing, they may exaggerate the reported benefits. That is a common concern in meta-analysis: **small studies tend to report larger effects** than larger studies, and when they are missing, the pooled estimate can be biased upward [N4-R5]. The excerpt from the sedentary behavior meta-analysis also notes that objective measurement is important because subjective methods reduce data accuracy, which implies that weak or biased studies may be more likely to be published and thus influence the overall evidence base [N4-F3]. However, the provided evidence does not include a direct meta-analysis of sedentary behavior interventions that explicitly confirms or denies missing studies in this exact context.

A limitation of meta-analysis when bias is present is that it may produce a misleadingly positive or homogeneous picture. The evidence here shows that some studies report **low or no publication bias** [N4-R2][N4-F3], while others report **asymmetric funnel plots and high Egger bias** [N4-R5]. This inconsistency means that the conclusion should be conservative: meta-analysis should be interpreted with caution when funnel plots are asymmetric or when Egger tests suggest potential bias, because the true effect size may differ from the reported one [N4-R5][N4-F3]. The provided evidence also supports the general methodological importance of bias detection, including funnel plots and Egger regression [N4-R3][N4-F3], which are standard tools for identifying small-study effects.

In summary, the available evidence suggests that publication bias and small-study effects can distort conclusions, but the direction and strength of distortion vary by study. Funnel plot asymmetry and a positive Egger test are signs of possible exaggeration of reported benefits [N4-R5][N4-F3], while some studies report low or no publication bias [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The limitation is that meta-analysis can be misleading if bias is present, and the evidence provided here is insufficient to determine whether missing studies in this specific intervention context exaggerate or reduce reported benefits across all subgroups [N4-R5][N4-F3].

The intervention evidence suggests that sedentary behavior interventions can increase standing time at work, but the magnitude, direction, and durability of effects vary. The most directly relevant evidence comes from a systematic review of workplace interventions, which found that **interventions using sit-stand desks, either alone or in combination with information and counseling, reduced sitting time at work on average by 100 minutes per workday at short-term follow-up** [N2-F2]. This same review also reports that sit-stand desks reduced sitting time by **57 minutes per day at medium-term follow-up** [N2-F2]. It also found that **short breaks reduced sitting time by 40 minutes per day at short-term follow-up**, while **computer prompting combined with instruction to stand** reduced sitting time by **14 minutes per day at short-term follow-up** [N2-F2]. These results indicate that interventions can meaningfully reduce sitting and may increase standing time, but the effect size depends on the intervention type.

The most effective interventions in workplace settings appear to be **multicomponent interventions** and **sit-stand desks with added support or delivery components**. The review notes that **multicomponent interventions had significant but heterogeneous effects on sitting time at work** [N2-F2]. It also reports that **the SWAL plus desk intervention** reduced sitting time by **63.7 minutes/day** at 12-month follow-up and was **threefold more effective** than the baseline SWAL intervention [N1-F1]. In addition, the broader workplace interventions review reports that **height-adjustable desks** and **multi-component interventions** were among the most promising approaches, with the multi-component intervention showing **significant reductions in sitting time over short, medium, and longer term** [N7-R5]. This suggests that interventions are more effective when they combine physical changes with organizational or behavioral strategies.

On durability, the evidence is strongest for interventions with longer follow-up. The **SMART Work and Life (SWAL) plus desk** intervention showed effects at **three and 12-month follow-ups**, with the most substantial reductions at 12 months [N1-F1]. The workplace interventions review similarly reports **medium-term follow-up** effects of **57 minutes/day** [N2-F2], and the broader evidence on workplace interventions also says that **SMArT Work successfully reduced sitting time over the short, medium, and longer term** [N7-R5]. However, the review also notes that most studies had **small sample sizes, lack of longer-term follow-up, and limited valid assessments of sedentary behavior**, which means the durability of effects may be overestimated in the literature [N1-F1]. In other words, the evidence supports sustained effects, but the certainty of those effects depends on follow-up length and study quality.

Overall, the intervention evidence indicates that standing time at work can improve with sedentary behavior interventions, especially sit-stand desks and multicomponent approaches. The largest and most durable effects are associated with **height-adjustable desks plus supportive delivery modes**, while effects on standing time appear to be closely tied to reductions in sitting time [N1-F1][N2-F2][N7-R5]. The evidence also shows that effects can persist over time, but the literature is still limited by small samples and short-term follow-up [N1-F1].

Heterogeneity in sedentary behavior interventions explains why some studies show large effects while others show none, and it shapes conclusions across workplace type, population, and intervention design. The strongest evidence comes from the workplace interventions review, which reports that interventions using **sit-stand desks, either alone or in combination with information and counseling**, reduced sitting time at work on average by **100 minutes per workday at short-term follow-up** [N2-F2]. However, the same review also notes that effects were **heterogeneous** and that **computer prompting combined with instruction to stand** reduced sitting time by **14 minutes per day at short-term follow-up**, while **computer prompting with instruction to walk** had a smaller effect [N2-F2]. This heterogeneity reflects differences in intervention design, including whether the intervention is **physical workstation-based, behavioral, or multi-component**.

The evidence also shows that different intervention types have different magnitudes. **Short breaks** reduced sitting time by **40 minutes/day at short-term follow-up**, while **standing desks and sit-stand desks** had **no significant difference** in reducing sitting time at work, and **active workstations** had **unclear or inconsistent effects** [N2-F2]. Computer prompting with instruction to stand had a **small effect** of **14 minutes/day**, while computer prompting with instruction to walk had a **smaller effect** at short-term follow-up [N2-F2]. These results indicate that the **delivery mode and intensity** of the intervention matter: some interventions are more effective when they combine standing prompts with broader support, while others are less effective as standalone prompts [N2-F2].

Moderators such as **duration, intensity, and delivery mode** are clearly present. The review reports **short-term** and **medium-term** follow-up effects, suggesting that effects may not be immediate or consistent over time [N2-F2]. It also notes that **multicomponent interventions** had **significant but heterogeneous effects** on sitting time at work, with very low-quality evidence [N2-F2]. The evidence further suggests that **delivery mode** matters: sit-stand desks with added support or delivery components are more effective than desk-only interventions [N2-F2]. A separate meta-analysis in office workers reported that **multicomponent interventions significantly reduced occupational sitting time**, supporting the importance of combining multiple strategies [N3-R1].

Subgroup differences are also evident. The workplace interventions review includes studies from **high-income countries** and reports a wide range of intervention types, including **physical workplace changes, workplace policy changes, information and counseling, and multi-component interventions** [N2-F2]. It also notes that **no studies specifically investigated standing meetings or walking meetings** on sitting time [N2-F2], which implies that the evidence base is uneven across intervention types. The meta-analysis on office workers similarly reports **office-based interventions** and notes that the primary outcome was sitting time at work per day, with secondary outcomes including cardiometabolic risk factors and work-related outcomes [N3-R2]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that effects vary by **workplace setting**, **type of intervention**, and whether the intervention is **single-component or multi-component** [N2-F2][N3-R1].

Why some studies show large effects and others show none is partly explained by these moderators. Interventions with more **active components, longer follow-up, and organizational support** tend to produce larger effects [N2-F2][N3-R1]. In contrast, interventions that are **brief, standalone, or poorly delivered** show smaller or inconsistent effects [N2-F2]. The evidence also suggests that **study quality** matters, as the workplace interventions review reports that many studies had **low-quality evidence** and that the evidence base is limited by **small sample sizes, lack of longer-term follow-up, and limited valid assessments of sedentary behavior** [N2-F2]. This means that heterogeneous findings may reflect true variation in effectiveness, methodological weakness, or incomplete reporting rather than a single uniform effect [N2-F2][N3-R1].

In conclusion, heterogeneity shapes intervention findings because effects depend on **workplace type, intervention design, duration, intensity, and delivery mode**. The strongest evidence supports **sit-stand desks and multi-component interventions**, while other modes such as computer prompts or short breaks have smaller effects. Some studies show large effects because they combine active components and organizational support, while others show none because the intervention is less intensive or poorly implemented [N2-F2][N3-R1].

What determines intervention success and implementation feasibility in workplace sedentary behavior interventions is a combination of **feasibility, acceptability, adoption barriers, organizational support, supervisor involvement, dose-response, and sustainability over time**. The evidence here indicates that these factors are central to whether interventions are adopted and whether their effects persist.

Feasibility and acceptability are important because interventions must be practical to implement. A pilot study protocol for a workplace intervention notes that the study aimed to examine the **feasibility, acceptability, and efficacy** of a tailored workplace intervention to reduce and break up sitting in office workers [N6-F4]. It also emphasizes that interventions should be developed using a systematic process informed by participant needs and frameworks like the **Behavior Change Wheel and APEASE criteria** [N6-F4]. This suggests that feasibility depends on whether the intervention is **practical, affordable, safe, and acceptable** to participants. The same source notes that organizations may be reluctant to implement interventions if productivity is negatively affected, highlighting a real barrier to adoption [N6-F4]. The evidence also notes that **productivity concerns** are important for adoption, implying that feasibility cannot be assessed only by health outcomes but must include organizational concerns [N6-F4].

Organizational support and supervisor involvement are repeatedly emphasized as critical. The pilot study explicitly mentions **manager support** as part of multi-component interventions [N6-F4]. Another source notes that **organizational support for reducing sedentary time was noted as essential in a short-term multicomponent intervention**, and that organizational support is also important for long-term implementation [N6-R5]. Supervisor involvement is also relevant because one intervention targeted sedentary behavior by providing active workstations to employees and involved **supervisors** in the intervention process [N6-R2]. This indicates that interventions are more likely to succeed when supervisors are engaged and when the organization supports the change.

Dose-response and sustainability are also important. The workplace interventions review reports that **computer prompting combined with instruction to stand** had a **14-minute/day reduction at short-term follow-up**, while **computer prompting with instruction to walk** had a smaller effect, suggesting that **intensity and delivery mode** matter [N2-F2]. The review also reports that **short breaks** reduced sitting time by **40 minutes/day** at short-term follow-up, while **medium-term follow-up** effects were smaller and less consistent [N2-F2]. This pattern supports a dose-response idea: more frequent or more intense interventions may have larger effects, but effects may diminish over time. The broader evidence on workplace interventions also says that **SMArT Work successfully reduced sitting time over the short, medium, and longer term**, indicating some durability [N7-R5]. However, the evidence base is limited by small sample sizes and short-term follow-up, so sustainability should not be overstated [N2-F2].

Sustainability over time is supported by the fact that some interventions show effects at **three and 12-month follow-ups**, such as the **SWAL plus desk** intervention [N1-F1], and by the broader workplace interventions review reporting **medium-term follow-up** effects [N2-F2]. However, the literature also notes that many studies lack **longer-term follow-up** and valid assessments of sedentary behavior, which limits confidence in long-term sustainability [N1-F1]. This means that effects can persist, but the evidence is still limited, and interventions are more likely to succeed when they are **integrated into work routines and supported by organizational structures**.

Overall, intervention success and feasibility depend on whether the intervention is **practical, acceptable, supported by supervisors and organizations, and delivered with sufficient intensity**. Organizational support is especially important because it helps overcome adoption barriers, while dose-response and sustainability suggest that effects may be stronger and more durable when interventions are **more active, better supported, and better integrated into work culture** [N6-F4][N6-R5][N2-F2][N7-R5].

### 1) What sedentary behaviour interventions do to standing time at work

The evidence suggests that sedentary behaviour interventions can increase standing time at work, but the effects vary by intervention type, setting, and follow-up period. The strongest evidence comes from workplace interventions, which show that **sit-stand desks, either alone or in combination with information and counseling, reduce sitting time at work on average by 100 minutes per workday at short-term follow-up** [N2-F2]. The same review also reports **57 minutes per day** at medium-term follow-up [N2-F2]. These results imply that interventions can increase standing time indirectly by reducing sitting time, though standing time is not measured separately in every study.

The most effective interventions in workplace settings appear to be **multicomponent interventions** and **sit-stand desks with added support or delivery components**. The **SMART Work and Life (SWAL) plus desk** intervention reduced sitting time by **63.7 minutes/day** at 12-month follow-up and was **threefold more effective** than the baseline SWAL intervention [N1-F1]. In addition, the broader workplace interventions review reports that **height-adjustable desks and multi-component interventions** were among the most promising approaches, with the multi-component intervention showing **significant reductions in sitting time over short, medium, and longer term** [N7-R5]. This suggests that interventions are more effective when they combine physical changes with organizational or behavioral strategies.

On durability, the evidence is strongest for interventions with longer follow-up. The **SWAL plus desk** intervention showed effects at **three and 12-month follow-ups**, with the most substantial reductions at 12 months [N1-F1]. The workplace interventions review similarly reports **medium-term follow-up** effects of **57 minutes/day** [N2-F2], and the broader evidence on workplace interventions also says that **SMArT Work successfully reduced sitting time over the short, medium, and longer term** [N7-R5]. However, the literature is limited by small sample sizes, lack of longer-term follow-up, and limited valid assessments of sedentary behavior [N2-F2]. In other words, the effects can persist, but the certainty of those effects depends on follow-up length and study quality.

Overall, the intervention evidence indicates that standing time at work can improve with sedentary behaviour interventions, especially sit-stand desks and multi-component approaches. The largest and most durable effects are associated with **height-adjustable desks plus supportive delivery modes**, while effects on standing time appear to be closely tied to reductions in sitting time [N1-F1][N2-F2][N7-R5].

---

### 2) Why heterogeneity shapes intervention findings

Heterogeneity explains why some studies show large effects and others show none. The evidence shows that interventions vary by **workplace type, population, and intervention design**. The workplace interventions review includes studies from **high-income countries** and reports a wide range of intervention types, including **physical workplace changes, workplace policy changes, information and counseling, and multi-component interventions** [N2-F2]. It also notes that **no studies specifically investigated standing meetings or walking meetings** on sitting time [N2-F2], implying an uneven evidence base.

A key moderator is **delivery mode and intensity**. The review reports that **short breaks** reduced sitting time by **40 minutes/day** at short-term follow-up, while **computer prompting combined with instruction to stand** reduced sitting time by **14 minutes/day** at short-term follow-up [N2-F2]. Computer prompting with instruction to walk had a smaller effect, suggesting that the **intensity and content of the intervention matter** [N2-F2]. This pattern supports the idea that interventions are more effective when they combine active components with broader support.

Other moderators include **duration and follow-up**. The review reports **short-term** and **medium-term** follow-up effects, suggesting that effects may not be immediate or consistent over time [N2-F2]. It also notes that **multicomponent interventions** had **significant but heterogeneous effects** on sitting time at work, with very low-quality evidence [N2-F2]. A separate meta-analysis in office workers reported that **multicomponent interventions significantly reduced occupational sitting time**, supporting the importance of combining multiple strategies [N3-R1].

Subgroup differences are also evident. The workplace interventions review shows that effects vary by **workplace setting** and **type of intervention**, with some interventions being more effective than others [N2-F2]. The meta-analysis on office workers similarly reports **office-based interventions** and notes that the primary outcome was sitting time at work per day, with secondary outcomes including cardiometabolic risk factors and work-related outcomes [N3-R2]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that effects depend on **workplace type, intervention design, duration, intensity, and delivery mode** [N2-F2][N3-R1].

Why some studies show large effects and others show none is partly explained by these moderators. Interventions with more **active components, longer follow-up, and organizational support** tend to produce larger effects [N2-F2][N3-R1]. In contrast, interventions that are **brief, standalone, or poorly delivered** show smaller or inconsistent effects [N2-F2]. The evidence also suggests that **study quality** matters, as the workplace interventions review reports that many studies had **low-quality evidence** and that the evidence base is limited by **small sample sizes, lack of longer-term follow-up, and limited valid assessments of sedentary behavior** [N2-F2]. This means that heterogeneous findings may reflect true variation in effectiveness, methodological weakness, or incomplete reporting rather than a single uniform effect [N2-F2][N3-R1].

---

### 3) How publication bias and small-study effects distort conclusions

Publication bias and small-study effects can distort conclusions about sedentary behaviour interventions by inflating or deflating apparent treatment effects. The evidence here is mixed: one systematic review and meta-analysis reports **low evidence for publication bias** based on funnel plot inspection, but the same source also says that funnel plots “graphically depict” bias detection methods and that Egger regression is used for Mendelian randomization bias detection [N4-F3]. Another study explicitly reports that **Egger’s tests showed no significant publication bias** for prevalence of sedentary behavior in individuals with obesity and physical inactivity [N4-R2]. In contrast, a separate search result states that a funnel plot was asymmetric and the publication bias was **high** according to Egger’s test [N4-R5]. These results are not directly comparable because the latter is a different study and topic, so they should be interpreted cautiously.

The direction of distortion depends on the nature of missing studies. If smaller studies are missing, they may exaggerate the reported benefits. That is a common concern in meta-analysis: **small studies tend to report larger effects** than larger studies, and when they are missing, the pooled estimate can be biased upward [N4-R5]. The provided evidence also notes that objective measurement is important because subjective methods reduce data accuracy, which implies that weak or biased studies may be more likely to be published and thus influence the overall evidence base [N4-F3]. However, the evidence does not include a direct meta-analysis of sedentary behaviour interventions that explicitly confirms or denies missing studies in this exact context.

A limitation of meta-analysis when bias is present is that it may produce a misleadingly positive or homogeneous picture. The evidence shows that some studies report **low or no publication bias** [N4-R2][N4-F3], while others report **asymmetric funnel plots and high Egger bias** [N4-R5]. This inconsistency means the conclusion should be conservative: meta-analysis should be interpreted with caution when funnel plots are asymmetric or when Egger tests suggest potential bias, because the true effect size may differ from the reported one [N4-R5][N4-F3]. The provided evidence also supports the general methodological importance of bias detection, including funnel plots and Egger regression [N4-R3][N4-F3], which are standard tools for identifying small-study effects.

In summary, the available evidence suggests that publication bias and small-study effects can distort conclusions, but the direction and strength of distortion vary by study. Funnel plot asymmetry and a positive Egger test are signs of possible exaggeration of reported benefits [N4-R5][N4-F3], while some studies report low or no publication bias [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The limitation is that meta-analysis can be misleading if bias is present, and the evidence provided here is insufficient to determine whether missing studies in this specific intervention context exaggerate or reduce reported benefits across all subgroups [N4-R5][N4-F3].

---

### 4) What determines intervention success and implementation feasibility

Intervention success and implementation feasibility depend on whether the intervention is **practical, acceptable, supported by supervisors and organizations, and delivered with sufficient intensity**. A pilot study protocol for a workplace intervention notes that the study aimed to examine the **feasibility, acceptability, and efficacy** of a tailored workplace intervention to reduce and break up sitting in office workers [N6-F4]. It also emphasizes that interventions should be developed using a systematic process informed by participant needs and frameworks like the **Behavior Change Wheel and APEASE criteria** [N6-F4]. This suggests that feasibility depends on whether the intervention is **practical, affordable, safe, and acceptable** to participants.

Organizational support and supervisor involvement are repeatedly emphasized as critical. The pilot study explicitly mentions **manager support** as part of multi-component interventions [N6-F4]. Another source notes that **organizational support for reducing sedentary time was noted as essential in a short-term multicomponent intervention**, and that organizational support is also important for long-term implementation [N6-R5]. Supervisor involvement is also relevant because one intervention targeted sedentary behavior by providing active workstations to employees and involved **supervisors** in the intervention process [N6-R2]. This indicates that interventions are more likely to succeed when supervisors are engaged and when the organization supports the change.

Dose-response and sustainability are also important. The workplace interventions review reports that **computer prompting combined with instruction to stand** had a **14-minute/day reduction at short-term follow-up**, while **computer prompting with instruction to walk** had a smaller effect, suggesting that **intensity and delivery mode** matter [N2-F2]. The review also reports that **short breaks** reduced sitting time by **40 minutes/day** at short-term follow-up, while **medium-term follow-up** effects were smaller and less consistent [N2-F2]. This pattern supports a dose-response idea: more frequent or more intense interventions may have larger effects, but effects may diminish over time. The broader evidence on workplace interventions also says that **SMArT Work successfully reduced sitting time over the short, medium, and longer term**, indicating some durability [N7-R5]. However, the evidence base is limited by small sample sizes and short-term follow-up, so sustainability should not be overstated [N2-F2].

Sustainability over time is supported by the fact that some interventions show effects at **three and 12-month follow-ups**, such as the **SWAL plus desk** intervention [N1-F1], and by the broader workplace interventions review reporting **medium-term follow-up** effects [N2-F2]. However, the literature also notes that many studies lack **longer-term follow-up** and valid assessments of sedentary behavior, which limits confidence in long-term sustainability [N1-F1]. This means that effects can persist, but the evidence is still limited, and interventions are more likely to succeed when they are **integrated into work routines and supported by organizational structures**.

---

### 5) Integrated conclusion

Overall, sedentary behaviour interventions can increase standing time at work, especially when interventions include **sit-stand desks or multi-component approaches** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N7-R5]. The most durable effects are associated with **height-adjustable desks plus supportive delivery modes**, while effects on standing time appear closely tied to reductions in sitting time [N1-F1][N2-F2][N7-R5]. However, the evidence base is heterogeneous, so the magnitude and direction of effects vary by **workplace type, intervention design, duration, intensity, and delivery mode** [N2-F2][N3-R1].

Heterogeneity explains why some studies show large effects and others show none. Interventions with more **active components, longer follow-up, and organizational support** tend to produce larger effects, while brief, standalone, or poorly delivered interventions show smaller or inconsistent effects [N2-F2][N3-R1]. Publication bias and small-study effects can also distort conclusions: funnel plot asymmetry and a positive Egger test are signs of possible exaggeration of reported benefits, while some studies report low or no publication bias [N4-R5][N4-F3]. This means that meta-analysis should be interpreted with caution when bias is present.

Finally, intervention success and implementation feasibility depend on **feasibility, acceptability, adoption barriers, organizational support, supervisor involvement, dose-response, and sustainability over time** [N6-F4][N6-R5][N2-F2][N7-R5]. Interventions are more likely to succeed when they are practical, supported by supervisors and organizations, and delivered with sufficient intensity. At the same time, sustainability remains uncertain because many studies lack long-term follow-up and valid assessments [N2-F2][N1-F1].

In short: interventions can increase standing time at work, but the size and durability of effects depend on the intervention, the workplace context, and the quality of implementation. Heterogeneity and publication bias make the evidence mixed, and the most reliable interventions are those that combine active physical changes with organizational support and sustained delivery [N2-F2][N3-R1][N4-R5][N6-F4].
